content: Efforts at the national level should focus on strengthening supply chains and developing effective systems for drug forecasting and monitoring. Healthcare providers must be educated and trained to maintain a high level of suspicion for histoplasmosis in individuals with advanced HIV disease. They should also be equipped to differentiate histoplasmosis from tuberculosis (TB) and other systemic fungal infections. National-level policy guidance is essential to improve the management of histoplasmosis in people living with HIV. Implementing these guidelines effectively requires supportive supervision systems and tools to aid in prescribing decisions. The guidelines are available as a web-based resource and are supported by peer-reviewed publications of systematic reviews that form the basis of the recommendations. Although initially developed with a focus on the Americas, these recommendations have global applicability and will be integrated into the next edition of the World Health Organization (WHO) consolidated guidelines on antiretroviral drug use for treating and preventing HIV infection. These consolidated guidelines are scheduled for review and updates every 2–3 years. Key dissemination steps include presenting the recommendations at international conferences, conducting workshops to support country-level adaptation, developing tools to assist countries in prioritizing resources, and organizing briefings and joint planning sessions with international and national partners. The adoption of these recommendations into national guidelines will be regularly evaluated. Several research questions have emerged from discussions within the Guideline Development Group and evidence reviews. These include evaluating the performance of antigen detection outside the context of advanced HIV disease, determining whether histoplasma antigen detection can be used as a screening tool for histoplasmosis in advanced HIV, and exploring whether new antibodies can improve antigen detection performance. Other questions include the potential utility of a histoplasma interferon-gamma release assay for screening latent histoplasmosis, preventing immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), and reducing the time to antiretroviral therapy initiation in newly diagnosed HIV patients. Research is also needed to assess the global burden of histoplasmosis, the role of recently developed lateral flow antigen detection as a diagnostic standard, and the impact of antigen detection on trends in HIV-associated histoplasmosis incidence and mortality. Additional areas of interest include defining disease severity, determining the safety of discontinuing antifungal maintenance therapy earlier than 12 months, and understanding the outcomes of treating TB and histoplasmosis co-infection. The optimal dose of liposomal amphotericin B for disseminated histoplasmosis in people living with HIV remains undetermined, and clinical trials are underway to evaluate different dosing regimens. The incidence and severity of IRIS should also be quantified prospectively. The guidelines were developed through a structured process led by PAHO/WHO, with input from external experts. Between May 2018 and October 2019, three groups contributed to the development: the WHO Steering Group, the independent Guideline Development Group, and the External Review Group. These groups included experts in histoplasmosis and HIV, with diverse perspectives from across WHO regions. Gender, equity, human rights, and community perspectives were integral to the process. Recommendations were formulated using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach, which considers the certainty of evidence, the balance of benefits and harms, values and preferences, resource implications, and feasibility. Decisions were made through consensus, and no voting was required. The draft guidelines underwent peer review by members of the Guideline Development Group and the External Review Group. Conflicts of interest were disclosed and managed according to WHO policy, and no conflicts warranted exclusion from discussions. The evidence was appraised using systematic reviews and meta-analyses, focusing on diagnostic accuracy, therapeutic efficacy, and the modification of HIV or TB therapy for co-infected individuals. The GRADE framework was used to assess the strength of recommendations, which could be either strong or conditional based on the certainty of evidence and other factors. Equity and human rights considerations were central to the guideline development process. Improving access to recommended interventions is expected to enhance equity and uphold human rights, particularly for marginalized or stigmatized groups with poor access to healthcare services. Point-of-care diagnostic tests for histoplasmosis can improve diagnosis and management, addressing barriers to access in these populations. A regional meeting on histoplasmosis in the Americas was held in Manaus, Brazil, in March 2019, with over 100 participants from 24 countries. Discussions focused on surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment in Latin America. While 65% of countries reported having rapid testing for histoplasmosis in at least one laboratory, access to liposomal amphotericin B was limited. Only two countries (Nicaragua and the United States) included histoplasmosis in their surveillance systems. A regional SWOT analysis identified challenges such as limited availability of diagnostic kits, lack of point-of-care testing, and insufficient awareness among healthcare practitioners. Opportunities include the development of point-of-care tests, price control initiatives by PAHO/WHO, and integration of histoplasmosis into national and international HIV and TB programs.
